When conflict between the US and Iran began in March, disruption in the Middle East put energy costs firmly back on the agenda for copper miners. As updated cost guidance has emerged, rising diesel prices have increasingly been cited as a source of pressure.
But is diesel really the biggest cost concern facing copper producers?
In this episode of Mined Over Matter, we look beyond the headlines to examine how higher diesel prices are feeding through to mine costs and why the impact can vary significantly by region and mine type.
While diesel remains an important part of the cost base, strong copper and by-product prices are helping producers absorb some of the pressure. The discussion explores why diesel exposure differs between open-pit and underground operations, and why the industry's current position looks different from previous periods of energy cost inflation.
The team also considers some of the other pressures emerging across the copper industry. Skilled labour shortages and wage pressure are becoming increasingly important issues in Chile, while acid costs, declining ore grades and more complex ore bodies could add further pressure to costs and production.
Looking ahead to 2027, these pressures could have important implications for mine economics and production. With producers investing to maintain output amid declining grades, labour pressures and changing input costs, understanding where cost and supply risks are emerging will be increasingly important.
In the full episode, we explore:

How higher diesel prices are affecting copper mine costs
Why the impact of diesel varies by region and mine type
The role of strong copper and by-product prices in supporting producer margins
Why skilled labour shortages and wage pressure are becoming increasingly important in Chile
How acid costs and contract renegotiations could feed into the cost base in 2027
The impact of declining ore grades and more complex ore bodies on costs and production
What these pressures could mean for copper mine supply in 2027
